<!-- site: execute -->

Part II of Mildenhall and Major's *Pricing Insurance Risk: Theory and Practice*
(Wiley, 2022) is chapters 8 to 11. It prices a portfolio in two ways:

- Classical (chapters 8 and 9): premium calculation principles on each unit or
  on the total, the portfolio constant cost of capital (CCoC), ruin theory and
  option pricing.
- Modern (chapters 10 and 11): the premium is a distortion of the loss capped at
  the assets, a spectral risk measure (SRM). The book calibrates five
  representative distortions to one target and compares them.

Exhibit numbers are the book's. The text belongs to the authors, and this guide
explains it in new words. Related guides:

- Risk measures (VaR, TVaR, coherence, the representations of an SRM):
  [Pricing Insurance Risk, Part I](pir-risk-measures.md).
- The split of a portfolio price over its units (the natural allocation, Part
  III of the book): [the case studies guide](pricing-insurance-risk-case-studies.md)
  and [CAS Monograph 15 reproduced](capital-modeling-monograph-15.md).



This is the R twin of the Python guide [`pir-portfolio-pricing.md`](pir-portfolio-pricing.md),
with the same sections, examples and numbers. The text under each R chunk is its
output; `R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R` requires each chunk to print exactly
that text. To render the page, install the R package (`remotes::install_github`,
see `R/prospicio/bootstrap.R`) and run
`quarto render docs/guides/pir-portfolio-pricing.qmd`.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(prospicio)
```

## 1. Two books to price

The practice chapters use the book's case studies. Two of them run fast enough
for a guide:

- **Tame** has two gamma units with mean 50 and CVs 0.10 and 0.15, at a 99.99%
  VaR capital standard. In the net view, an aggregate cover of 12.91 excess of
  56.17 applies to unit B.
- **Cat/Non-Cat** has a gamma Non-Cat unit (mean 80, CV 0.15) and a lognormal
  Cat unit (mean 20, CV 1), at 99.9%. In the net view, 79.64 excess of 41.11
  applies to Cat (Table 7.3).

The code puts each unit on the grid of `aggregate`, with a step of 1/64 and
2^16 points. A net unit is the gross unit minus the recovery of the cover,
outcome by outcome:

```{r}
started <- Sys.time()
STEP <- 1 / 64
POINTS <- 2^16

# A severity on aggregate's grid: rounded, the mass above the top spread by renormalizing.
discretize_renormalized <- function(severity) {
  probs <- discretize(severity, STEP, 2 * POINTS, method = "rounding")@probs[seq_len(POINTS)]
  grid_distribution(STEP, probs / sum(probs))
}

# The grid's loss less an aggregate cover of limit excess of attachment.
net_of <- function(grid, limit, attachment) {
  map_grid(grid, function(x) x - pmin(pmax(x - attachment, 0), limit))$grid
}

# The total of a portfolio as a grid.
total_grid <- function(book) {
  idx <- round(book@totals / STEP) + 1
  probs <- tapply(book@probs, factor(idx, levels = seq_len(max(idx))), sum)
  grid_distribution(STEP, ifelse(is.na(probs), 0, probs))
}

# Python's repr of a float, for the book's printed values: 102.0 rather than 102.
pyfloat <- function(x) ifelse(x == round(x), sprintf("%.1f", x), as.character(x))
pylist <- function(x) paste0("[", paste(pyfloat(x), collapse = ", "), "]")

a_unit <- discretize_renormalized(gamma_from_mean_cv(50, 0.10))
b_unit <- discretize_renormalized(gamma_from_mean_cv(50, 0.15))
b_net <- net_of(b_unit, 12.91, 56.17)
tame <- capital_portfolio(list(A = a_unit, B = b_unit))
tame_net <- capital_portfolio(list(A = a_unit, B = b_net))

cat_unit <- discretize_renormalized(lognormal_from_mean_cv(20, 1))
non_cat <- discretize_renormalized(gamma_from_mean_cv(80, 0.15))
cat_net <- net_of(cat_unit, 79.64, 41.11)
cnc <- capital_portfolio(list(Cat = cat_unit, NonCat = non_cat))
cnc_net <- capital_portfolio(list(Cat = cat_net, NonCat = non_cat))

cat(sprintf("means: B net %.3f (book 49.08), Cat net %.3f (book 17.79)\n", mean(b_net), mean(cat_net)))
```

```text
means: B net 49.084 (book 49.08), Cat net 17.786 (book 17.79)
```

The covers are quantiles of the gross units: 80% and 99% of B (56.17, 69.08),
90% and 99.5% of Cat (41.11, 120.75). `map_grid()` puts the net unit exactly on
the grid. `tower_on_grid()` gives the same distribution by FFT, with the FFT
round-off (about 1e-19) set to zero. Section 3 shows why that matters.

## 2. The portfolio CCoC price

Chapter 8's classical portfolio price is the benchmark of every practice
chapter. Assets are the VaR of the total, and the premium charges a constant
cost of capital on the capital: P = v E[min(X, a)] + d a, with v = 1 / 1.1 and
d = 1 - v at a 10% return. The insurance pentagon gives the margin, capital,
loss ratio and leverage.

Table 7.2 gives the result for each book. Leverage is premium to capital
(`premium_to_capital` in `natural_price()`). The loss is the expected loss within
the assets, so it includes default (Cat/Non-Cat gross: 99.95, not 100). All 24
figures agree:

```{r}
#| label: table-72
library(gt)

# A table whose rows alternate prospicio and the book: prospicio at fixed decimals, the book as printed.
pair_table <- function(frame, decimals) {
  own_rows <- seq(1, nrow(frame), by = 2)
  book_rows <- seq(2, nrow(frame), by = 2)
  table <- gt(frame, rowname_col = names(frame)[1])
  for (column in names(decimals)) {
    table <- table |>
      fmt_number(columns = all_of(column), rows = own_rows, decimals = decimals[[column]], use_seps = FALSE) |>
      fmt_number(columns = all_of(column), rows = book_rows, decimals = 4, drop_trailing_zeros = TRUE, use_seps = FALSE)
  }
  sub_missing(table, missing_text = "")
}

ccoc <- distortion("ccoc", 0.10)
BOOK_72 <- list( # Table 7.2: loss, margin, premium, capital, assets, leverage
  c(100.00, 3.42, 103.4, 34.23, 137.7, 3.02),
  c(99.08, 2.46, 101.5, 24.64, 126.2, 4.12),
  c(99.95, 15.21, 115.2, 152.1, 267.2, 0.757),
  c(97.73, 8.17, 105.9, 81.68, 187.6, 1.3)
)
BOOKS <- list(
  list(name = "Tame", view = "gross", book = tame, p = 0.9999),
  list(name = "Tame", view = "net", book = tame_net, p = 0.9999),
  list(name = "Cat/Non-Cat", view = "gross", book = cnc, p = 0.999),
  list(name = "Cat/Non-Cat", view = "net", book = cnc_net, p = 0.999)
)
BOOK_NAMES <- sapply(BOOKS, function(b) paste(b$name, b$view))
interleave <- function(mine, book) as.vector(rbind(mine, paste0(mine, ", book")))
total_row <- function(prices) prices[prices$unit == "total", ]
COLUMNS_72 <- c("loss", "margin", "premium", "capital", "assets", "P/Q")
rows <- list()
for (k in seq_along(BOOKS)) {
  b <- BOOKS[[k]]
  t <- total_row(natural_price(b$book, ccoc, p = b$p))
  rows[[2 * k - 1]] <- c(t$loss, t$margin, t$premium, t$capital, t$assets, t$premium_to_capital)
  rows[[2 * k]] <- BOOK_72[[k]]
}
table_72 <- data.frame(book = interleave(BOOK_NAMES), do.call(rbind, rows), check.names = FALSE)
names(table_72)[-1] <- COLUMNS_72
pair_table(table_72, c(setNames(rep(2, 5), COLUMNS_72[1:5]), `P/Q` = 3)) |>
  tab_header("Table 7.2: the portfolio CCoC price", "Currency units; P/Q is premium over capital")
```

```text
                           loss  margin  premium  capital  assets    P/Q
Tame gross               100.00    3.42   103.42    34.23  137.66  3.021
Tame gross, book            100    3.42    103.4    34.23   137.7   3.02
Tame net                  99.08    2.46   101.55    24.64  126.19  4.121
Tame net, book            99.08    2.46    101.5    24.64   126.2   4.12
Cat/Non-Cat gross         99.95   15.21   115.15   152.05  267.20  0.757
Cat/Non-Cat gross, book   99.95   15.21    115.2    152.1   267.2  0.757
Cat/Non-Cat net           97.73    8.17   105.90    81.68  187.58  1.297
Cat/Non-Cat net, book     97.73    8.17    105.9    81.68   187.6    1.3
```

Stand-alone, each unit holds its own 99.99% or 99.9% VaR, so the units together
need more capital than the book (Tables 9.12, 9.13 and 9.11). B and Cat are net
of their cover in the net rows. P is premium and Q is capital:

```{r}
#| label: table-sa
BOOK_SA <- list( # Tables 9.12, 9.13: stand-alone premium and capital by unit; Table 9.11's sums
  list(c(51.89, 52.98), c(18.88, 29.82), 104.9, 48.69),
  list(c(51.89, 50.98), c(18.88, 18.91), 102.9, 37.79),
  list(c(34.98, 83.84), c(150.3, 38.41), 118.8, 188.7),
  list(c(25.72, 83.84), c(79.92, 38.41), 109.6, 118.3)
)
rows <- list()
for (k in seq_along(BOOKS)) {
  b <- BOOKS[[k]]
  sa <- price_stand_alone(b$book, ccoc, b$p)
  units <- sa[1:2, ]
  s <- sa[sa$unit == "sum", ]
  t <- sa[sa$unit == "total", ]
  bk <- BOOK_SA[[k]]
  rows[[2 * k - 1]] <- c(units$premium[1], units$capital[1], units$premium[2], units$capital[2],
                         s$premium, t$premium, t$premium / s$premium - 1,
                         s$capital, t$capital, t$capital / s$capital - 1)
  rows[[2 * k]] <- c(bk[[1]][1], bk[[2]][1], bk[[1]][2], bk[[2]][2], bk[[3]], NA, NA, bk[[4]], NA, NA)
}
table_sa <- data.frame(book = interleave(BOOK_NAMES), do.call(rbind, rows))
names(table_sa)[-1] <- c("p1", "q1", "p2", "q2", "sum_p", "total_p", "saved_p", "sum_q", "total_q", "saved_q")
pair_table(table_sa, setNames(rep(2, 8), c("p1", "q1", "p2", "q2", "sum_p", "total_p", "sum_q", "total_q"))) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c("saved_p", "saved_q"), rows = seq(1, nrow(table_sa), by = 2), decimals = 1) |>

  tab_spanner("unit 1", columns = c("p1", "q1")) |>
  tab_spanner("unit 2", columns = c("p2", "q2")) |>
  tab_spanner("premium", columns = c("sum_p", "total_p", "saved_p")) |>
  tab_spanner("capital", columns = c("sum_q", "total_q", "saved_q")) |>
  cols_label(p1 = "P", q1 = "Q", p2 = "P", q2 = "Q", sum_p = "sum of units", total_p = "total",
             saved_p = "change", sum_q = "sum of units", total_q = "total", saved_q = "change")
```

Premium falls less than capital, because most of it is expected loss and pooling
does not change that. The thin tails of Tame give the most diversification.

## 3. Classical premium principles

Section 9.1 applies ten of the premium calculation principles of section 8.4
(PCPs). Each is calibrated so that the gross total costs the CCoC premium above,
then applied stand-alone to each unit, to the net units and to the net total.
prospicio has them as `classical_premium(x, principle, loading)`;
`calibrate_classical()` finds a loading. The book's Fischer principle uses the
power 2, the prospicio default.

Table 9.2 lists the Tame premiums, sorted by the net total, with the book's
loading. The last column is the largest gap to the book's premiums in the row:

```{r}
#| label: table-92
PRINCIPLES <- c("expected_value", "variance", "esscher", "exponential", "semi_variance",
                "var", "dutch", "standard_deviation", "fischer")
BOOK_92 <- list( # Table 9.2, Tame: loading; A, B net, B gross, total net, total gross
  expected_value = c(0.034, 51.712, 50.765, 51.712, 102.476, 103.423),
  variance = c(0.042, 51.053, 50.620, 52.370, 101.673, 103.423),
  esscher = c(0.041, 51.034, 50.468, 52.389, 101.503, 103.423),
  exponential = c(0.080, 51.028, 50.420, 52.395, 101.447, 103.423),
  semi_variance = c(0.080, 51.051, 50.330, 52.425, 101.411, 103.423),
  var = c(0.659, 51.906, 52.750, 52.750, 102.672, 103.422),
  dutch = c(0.953, 51.899, 51.498, 52.846, 102.096, 103.423),
  standard_deviation = c(0.380, 51.899, 51.377, 52.848, 102.061, 103.423),
  fischer = c(0.523, 51.897, 51.149, 52.881, 101.907, 103.423)
)

# Each principle's loading and premiums on the grids, with the book's loading and the largest gap.
classical_frame <- function(gross_total, grids, labels, target, book_values) {
  rows <- lapply(names(book_values), function(principle) {
    book <- book_values[[principle]]
    t <- calibrate_classical(gross_total, principle, target)
    got <- sapply(grids, function(g) classical_premium(g, principle, t))
    c(t, book[1], got, max(abs(got - book[-1])))
  })
  frame <- data.frame(principle = gsub("_", " ", names(book_values)), do.call(rbind, rows), check.names = FALSE)
  names(frame)[-1] <- c("loading", "book loading", labels, "gap")
  frame[order(frame$net), ]
}

classical_gt <- function(frame, title, subtitle, spanned) {
  table <- gt(frame, rowname_col = "principle") |>
    tab_header(title, subtitle) |>
    tab_spanner("calibrated loading", columns = c("loading", "book loading")) |>
    fmt_number(columns = everything(), decimals = 3) |>
    cols_label(loading = "prospicio", `book loading` = "book")
  for (label in names(spanned)) table <- tab_spanner(table, label, columns = spanned[[label]])
  table
}

tame_target <- total_row(natural_price(tame, ccoc, p = 0.9999))$premium
tame_total <- total_grid(tame)
tame_net_total <- total_grid(tame_net)
tame_92 <- classical_frame(tame_total, list(a_unit, b_net, b_unit, tame_net_total, tame_total),
                           c("A", "B net", "B", "net", "total"), tame_target, BOOK_92)
classical_gt(tame_92, "Table 9.2: Tame premiums by principle, each calibrated to the CCoC total",
             "Currency units; the loading is the parameter of the principle",
             list(units = c("A", "B net", "B"), totals = c("net", "total")))
```

Loadings and premiums agree to the third decimal (0.001 is rounding).

Table 9.3 subtracts the pooled premium from the sum of the stand-alone premiums
(SoP). The book prints the gross SoP for every principle but expected value:

```{r}
#| label: table-93
BOOK_93 <- c(variance = 103.423, esscher = 103.423, exponential = 103.423, semi_variance = 103.477,
             var = 104.656, dutch = 104.745, standard_deviation = 104.747, fischer = 104.778)
rows <- lapply(PRINCIPLES, function(principle) {
  t <- calibrate_classical(tame_total, principle, tame_target)
  sop <- classical_premium(a_unit, principle, t) + classical_premium(b_unit, principle, t)
  sop_net <- classical_premium(a_unit, principle, t) + classical_premium(b_net, principle, t)
  net <- classical_premium(tame_net_total, principle, t)
  c(sop, sop - tame_target, unname(BOOK_93[principle]), sop_net, sop_net - net)
})
table_93 <- data.frame(principle = gsub("_", " ", PRINCIPLES), do.call(rbind, rows))
names(table_93)[-1] <- c("sop", "delta", "book", "sop_net", "delta_net")
gt(table_93, rowname_col = "principle") |>
  tab_header("Table 9.3: stand-alone sum less the pooled premium", "Tame; currency units") |>
  tab_spanner("gross", columns = c("sop", "delta", "book")) |>
  tab_spanner("net", columns = c("sop_net", "delta_net")) |>
  fmt_number(columns = everything(), decimals = 3) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "") |>
  cols_label(sop = "SoP", delta = "delta", book = "book SoP", sop_net = "SoP", delta_net = "delta")
```

```text
                        SoP  delta  book SoP      SoP   delta
expected value      103.423  0.000            102.476   0.000
variance            103.423  0.000   103.423  101.672   0.000
esscher             103.423  0.000   103.423  101.502   0.000
exponential         103.423  0.000   103.423  101.447   0.000
semi variance       103.477  0.054   103.477  101.381  -0.030
var                 104.656  1.233   104.656  104.656   1.984
dutch               104.745  1.322   104.745  103.397   1.301
standard deviation  104.747  1.324   104.747  103.275   1.214
fischer             104.778  1.355   104.778  103.046   1.140
```

The deltas show that the formula of a principle, not the data, sets its view of
diversification:

- Expected value, variance, Esscher and exponential are additive for
  independent units, so pooling earns nothing.
- VaR and the deviation principles (Dutch, standard deviation, Fischer) are
  subadditive. They charge the pool about 1.3 less than the parts.
- The semivariance is neither. Its delta changes sign between gross and net
  (0.054 and -0.029 in the book).

Two principles are sensitive to how the net B grid is made. The exponential and
Esscher premiums weight an outcome x by exp(t x). On a grid to 1,024,
exp(0.08 x) is about 1e35 at the top, so an FFT round-off of 1e-19 there would
give a premium of hundreds. `tower_on_grid()` sets probabilities below machine
epsilon to zero, as `aggregate`'s `remove_fuzz` does, so its net grid prices like
the exact grid:

```{r}
cover <- reinsurance_tower(list(aggregate_stop_loss("B", 12.91, 56.17)))
b_net_fft <- tower_on_grid(cover, fixed_count(1), b_unit, POINTS)$net
t_exp <- calibrate_classical(tame_total, "exponential", tame_target)
fft_premium <- classical_premium(b_net_fft, "exponential", t_exp)
noise <- max(b_net_fft@probs[-seq_len(150 * 64)])
cat(sprintf("exponential premium of net B: by map %.3f, from the FFT %.3f (book 50.420)\n",
            classical_premium(b_net, "exponential", t_exp), fft_premium))
cat(sprintf("largest probability above 150: FFT %s, map exactly zero\n",
            if (noise == 0) "exactly zero" else noise))
```

```text
exponential premium of net B: by map 50.419, from the FFT 50.419 (book 50.420)
largest probability above 150: FFT exactly zero, map exactly zero
```

For a grid from another source (for example, your own FFT), call
`remove_fuzz()` before you price with these two principles.

On Cat/Non-Cat, the principles differ much more (Tables 9.5 and 9.6):

```{r}
  expected_value = c(0.152, 20.480, 23.030, 92.121, 112.601, 115.151),
  var = c(0.818, 30.109, 30.109, 90.734, 113.391, 115.141),
  variance = c(0.028, 22.573, 31.141, 84.013, 106.585, 115.151),
```


Seven principles agree to within 0.003, the difference that two truncations of
a lognormal tail give. Esscher and exponential do not, and should not:

```{r}
#| label: table-exp
BOOK_EXP <- list(esscher = c(0.011, 23.575, 35.944, 81.561, 105.054),
                 exponential = c(0.014, 24.760, 39.697, 81.059, 105.619))
rows <- list()
for (principle in names(BOOK_EXP)) {
  t <- calibrate_classical(cnc_total, principle, cnc_target)
  got <- sapply(list(cat_net, cat_unit, non_cat, cnc_net_total), function(g) classical_premium(g, principle, t))
  rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- c(t, got)
  rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- BOOK_EXP[[principle]]
}
table_exp <- data.frame(principle = interleave(names(BOOK_EXP)), do.call(rbind, rows), check.names = FALSE)
names(table_exp)[-1] <- c("loading", "Cat net", "Cat", "Non-Cat", "net")
pair_table(table_exp, c(loading = 4, `Cat net` = 3, Cat = 3, `Non-Cat` = 3, net = 3)) |>
  tab_header("Esscher and exponential premiums on Cat/Non-Cat", "Currency units; the book's values are as printed")
```

```text
                   loading  Cat net     Cat  Non-Cat      net
esscher             0.0103   22.760  33.639   81.512  104.272
esscher, book        0.011   23.575  35.944   81.561  105.054
exponential         0.0138   22.820  34.139   81.012  103.832
exponential, book    0.014    24.76  39.697   81.059  105.619
```

```{r}
lower <- cat_unit@probs[seq_len(POINTS / 2)]
top_half <- grid_distribution(STEP, lower / sum(lower))
cat(sprintf("exponential premium of Cat at loading 0.014: grid to 1,024 %.3f, grid to 512 %.3f\n",
            classical_premium(cat_unit, "exponential", 0.014), classical_premium(top_half, "exponential", 0.014)))
```

```text
exponential premium of Cat at loading 0.014: grid to 1,024 35.497, grid to 512 25.189
```

A lognormal has no exponential moment: E[exp(t X)] is infinite for every t > 0,
so both premiums are artifacts of where the grid stops. The book does not apply
them to the Hurricane/SCS case for this reason. Do not use them for a loss
without a light tail.

## 4. Ruin theory and the natural scale of a market

Section 9.3 uses the Pollaczeck-Khinchine formula for the probability of
eventual ruin of a compound Poisson surplus process (`eventual_ruin()` and its
`capital_interpolated`). The example is a liability line with lognormal claims
of mean 50,000 and CV 10, limited at 1M, 5M or 10M.

With a margin r on expected loss, the formula gives the starting surplus u at
which eventual ruin has probability p. The annual margin, n r E[X] for n claims
a year, must pay a cost of capital delta on u, so a market needs at least
n = delta u / (r E[X]) claims a year (Eq. (9.2)). Table 9.15 gives n for
delta = 0.1:

```{r}
#| label: table-915
claim <- lognormal_from_mean_cv(50000, 10)
BOOK_915 <- list( # Table 9.15: limit -> p -> n at r = 0.05, 0.1, 0.25
  list(limit = 1e6, book = list(`0.01` = c(10172, 2655, 476.1), `0.1` = c(5021, 1294, 224.5))),
  list(limit = 1e7, book = list(`0.01` = c(33610, 9087, 1765), `0.1` = c(16384, 4324, 793.6)))
)
RUIN_P <- c(0.01, 0.1)
rows <- list()
cases <- character()
for (row in BOOK_915) {
  limit <- row$limit
  # 10,000 steps up to the limit; the claim's mass above the limit lands on it
  capped <- map_grid(discretize(claim, limit / 10000, 10001, method = "rounding"), function(x) pmin(x, limit))$grid
  counts <- sapply(c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25), function(r) {  # one row per p, one column per r
    u <- eventual_ruin(capped, rho = r, p = RUIN_P, points = 2^18)$capital_interpolated
    0.1 * u / (r * mean(capped))
  })
  for (i in seq_along(RUIN_P)) {
    book <- row$book[[i]]
    cases <- c(cases, sprintf("%s, p %s", formatC(limit, format = "d", big.mark = ","), RUIN_P[i]))
    rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- c(counts[i, ], book, book / counts[i, ])
  }
}
table_915 <- data.frame(case = cases, do.call(rbind, rows))
names(table_915)[-1] <- c("n1", "n2", "n3", "b1", "b2", "b3", "x1", "x2", "x3")
gt(table_915, rowname_col = "case") |>
  tab_header("Table 9.15: claims a year a market needs", "By limit and ruin probability p, at margins r = 5%, 10%, 25%") |>
  tab_spanner("prospicio", columns = c("n1", "n2", "n3")) |>
  tab_spanner("book", columns = c("b1", "b2", "b3")) |>
  tab_spanner("book / prospicio", columns = c("x1", "x2", "x3")) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c("n1", "n2", "n3"), decimals = 1, use_seps = FALSE) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c("b1", "b2", "b3"), decimals = 1, drop_trailing_zeros = TRUE, use_seps = FALSE) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(n1 = "5%", n2 = "10%", n3 = "25%", b1 = "5%", b2 = "10%", b3 = "25%", x1 = "5%", x2 = "10%", x3 = "25%")
```

```text
                        5%    10%    25%     5%   10%    25%     5%    10%    25%
1,000,000, p 0.01   1019.0  266.0   47.7  10172  2655  476.1   9.98   9.98   9.98
1,000,000, p 0.1     503.0  129.7   22.5   5021  1294  224.5   9.98   9.98   9.99
10,000,000, p 0.01  3362.0  909.0  176.5  33610  9087   1765  10.00  10.00  10.00
10,000,000, p 0.1   1639.0  432.5   79.4  16384  4324  793.6  10.00  10.00  10.00
```

Every prospicio count is one tenth of the book's. The book's table is
u / (r E[X]), Eq. (9.2) with delta = 1, so it seems to omit the cost of capital
of 0.1 that its caption gives. The text example has the same factor: 39,776
claims, about 800,000 policies, for a 1M limit at p = 0.01 and r = 0.025. The
factor is constant, so the book's conclusions about the scale hold. (The grid
causes the remaining 0.2%.)

## 5. The modern view: a price for each layer of assets

Chapter 10 starts from the layer. The risk that losses consume the l-th unit of
assets is a Bernoulli with probability s = S(l), priced at g(s), where g is a
distortion. Summed over the layers, this is the premium for a loss X with assets
a: the integral of g(S(x)) from 0 to a, the SRM of the capped loss X ^ a.

A Bernoulli layer has expected loss s, premium g(s), margin g(s) - s and
capital 1 - g(s). Its loss ratio is s / g(s), its return on capital
(g(s) - s) / (1 - g(s)), and its premium leverage g(s) / (1 - g(s)). Exercise 142
tabulates these for the proportional hazard distortions s^rho (Table 10.3). The
last column is the largest gap to the book:

```{r}
#| label: table-103
BOOK_103 <- list( # Table 10.3 at s = 0.01, 0.1, 0.5: loss ratio, risk return, premium leverage
  `0.4` = list(c(0.0631, 0.2512, 0.6598), c(0.1765, 0.4953, 1.0649), c(0.1883, 0.6614, 3.1298)),
  `0.5` = list(c(0.1000, 0.3162, 0.7071), c(0.1000, 0.3162, 0.7071), c(0.1111, 0.4625, 2.4142)),
  `0.7` = list(c(0.2512, 0.5012, 0.8123), c(0.0310, 0.1243, 0.3006), c(0.0415, 0.2493, 1.6013)),
  `0.9` = list(c(0.6310, 0.7943, 0.9330), c(0.0059, 0.0296, 0.0773), c(0.0161, 0.1440, 1.1546))
)
S <- c(0.01, 0.1, 0.5)
rows <- lapply(names(BOOK_103), function(rho) {
  gs <- distortion_g(distortion("proportional_hazard", as.numeric(rho)), S)
  stats <- list(S / gs, (gs - S) / (1 - gs), gs / (1 - gs))
  c(unlist(stats), max(abs(unlist(stats) - unlist(BOOK_103[[rho]]))))
})
names_103 <- paste0(rep(c("lr", "roc", "lev"), each = 3), 1:3)
table_103 <- data.frame(rho = paste("rho", names(BOOK_103)), do.call(rbind, rows))
names(table_103)[-1] <- c(names_103, "gap")
gt(table_103, rowname_col = "rho") |>
  tab_header("Table 10.3: Bernoulli layers under the proportional hazard", "At s = 0.01, 0.1 and 0.5") |>
  tab_spanner("loss ratio", columns = names_103[1:3]) |>
  tab_spanner("return on capital", columns = names_103[4:6]) |>
  tab_spanner("premium leverage", columns = names_103[7:9]) |>
  fmt_number(columns = everything(), decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(.list = setNames(as.list(paste("s =", rep(S, 3))), names_103))
```

```text
         s = 0.01  s = 0.1  s = 0.5  s = 0.01  s = 0.1  s = 0.5  s = 0.01  s = 0.1  s = 0.5     gap
rho 0.4    0.0631   0.2512   0.6598    0.1765   0.4953   1.0649    0.1883   0.6614   3.1298  0.0000
rho 0.5    0.1000   0.3162   0.7071    0.1000   0.3162   0.7071    0.1111   0.4625   2.4142  0.0000
rho 0.7    0.2512   0.5012   0.8123    0.0310   0.1243   0.3006    0.0415   0.2493   1.6013  0.0000
rho 0.9    0.6310   0.7943   0.9330    0.0059   0.0296   0.0773    0.0161   0.1440   1.1546  0.0000
```

The main lesson of the chapter: a concave g charges remote layers (small s) a
low loss ratio, but they need much capital for each unit of premium, so their
return is also low. The return on capital increases with s. Only the CCoC
distortion, a straight line from (0, d) to (1, 1), earns the same return on
every layer. Hence "constant".

Return on capital of a layer against its exceedance probability s:

```{r}
#| label: return-on-capital-figure
library(ggplot2, exclude = "layer")   # keeps prospicio's layer()
grid_s <- 10^seq(-3, -0.01, length.out = 100)
roc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  list("PH, rho 0.5" = distortion("proportional_hazard", 0.5),
       "PH, rho 0.7" = distortion("proportional_hazard", 0.7),
       "CCoC, 10%" = distortion("ccoc", 0.10)),
  function(d) {
    gs <- distortion_g(d, grid_s)
    data.frame(s = grid_s, roc = (gs - grid_s) / (1 - gs))
  }))
roc$distortion <- factor(rep(c("PH, rho 0.5", "PH, rho 0.7", "CCoC, 10%"), each = length(grid_s)),
                         levels = c("PH, rho 0.5", "PH, rho 0.7", "CCoC, 10%"))
ggplot(roc, aes(s, roc, colour = distortion)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "exceedance probability s of the layer", y = "return on capital of the layer",
       colour = NULL, title = "Return on capital by layer") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Premium of the Simple Discrete Example of Part I as a function of the assets,
under the PH with rho 0.5 (book values from Tables 11.1 and 11.3):

```{r}
#| label: table-cap
OUTCOMES <- c(0, 1, 8, 9, 10, 11, 90, 98, 100)
SIXTEENTHS <- c(4, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1)
draws <- rep(OUTCOMES, SIXTEENTHS)
ph <- distortion("proportional_hazard", 0.5)
rows <- lapply(c(10, 50, 80, 90, 100), function(a) {
  capped <- sampled(pmin(draws, a))
  premium <- risk_measure(capped, ph)
  book <- c(`80` = 42.828, `100` = 51.156)[as.character(a)]
  c(mean(capped), premium, unname(book), premium - mean(capped), a - premium)
})
table_cap <- data.frame(assets = c("10", "50", "80", "90", "100"), do.call(rbind, rows))
names(table_cap)[-1] <- c("mean", "premium", "book", "margin", "capital")
gt(table_cap, rowname_col = "assets") |>
  tab_header("Premium of the loss capped at the assets", "PH with rho 0.5 on the Simple Discrete Example") |>
  fmt_number(columns = everything(), decimals = 3) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "") |>
  cols_label(mean = "E[X ^ a]", premium = "PH premium", book = "book premium")
```

```text
     E[X ^ a]  PH premium  book premium  margin  capital
10      6.062       7.769                 1.706    2.231
50     16.125      27.828                11.703   22.172
80     23.625      42.828        42.828  19.203   37.172
90     26.125      47.828                21.703   42.172
100    27.250      51.156        51.156  23.906   48.844
```

Premium funds most of the low layers, because losses consume them in most
outcomes. From 11 to 90, losses consume each added unit of assets only in the
25% of outcomes above 11, so each unit adds g(0.25) = 0.5 of premium and 0.5 of
capital. The top layers add mostly capital.

## 6. Calibrating the five distortions

Chapter 11 compares SRMs that charge the same total premium. The five families
are CCoC, proportional hazard (PH), Wang, dual power and TVaR, calibrated to the
gross CCoC premium of section 2. A sixth, "Blend", is piecewise linear and built
from layer costs of capital. Table 11.5 prints the calibrated parameters:

```{r}
#| label: table-115
FAMILIES <- c("ccoc", "ph", "wang", "dual", "tvar")
BOOK_115 <- list(Tame = c(0.10, 0.683, 0.375, 1.576, 0.227), `Cat/Non-Cat` = c(0.10, 0.596, 0.611, 2.463, 0.482))
fitted <- list()
rows <- list()
for (b in list(list(name = "Tame", book = tame, p = 0.9999), list(name = "Cat/Non-Cat", book = cnc, p = 0.999))) {
  fitted[[b$name]] <- sapply(FAMILIES, function(f) calibrate_portfolio(b$book, f, p = b$p, return_on_capital = 0.10),
                             simplify = FALSE)
  rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- unname(sapply(fitted[[b$name]], function(d) d@param[1]))
  rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- BOOK_115[[b$name]]
}
table_115 <- data.frame(book = interleave(names(BOOK_115)), do.call(rbind, rows))
names(table_115)[-1] <- FAMILIES
pair_table(table_115, setNames(rep(3, 5), FAMILIES)) |>
  tab_header("Table 11.5: calibrated parameters", "Each family calibrated to the gross CCoC premium")
```

```text
                    ccoc     ph   wang   dual   tvar
Tame               0.100  0.683  0.375  1.576  0.227
Tame, book           0.1  0.683  0.375  1.576  0.227
Cat/Non-Cat        0.100  0.596  0.611  2.463  0.482
Cat/Non-Cat, book    0.1  0.596  0.611  2.463  0.482
```

All ten parameters agree. `calibrate_portfolio()` returns a `distortion()`. Its
`param` is the return r for `"ccoc"`, the exponent rho for PH, the shift lambda
for Wang, the exponent beta for dual power and the level p for TVaR.

The case studies guide runs both books at 99.9% against `aggregate` 0.30.1; the
book's Tame uses 99.99%.

The Blend of Exercise 197 (Table 11.6) sets a layer cost of capital nu at some
exceedance probabilities s, from 2% for the most remote layers to 10% at
s = 0.2. At each point g(s) = (s + nu) / (1 + nu), and the Blend interpolates
between them. `distortion_convex()` builds the smallest concave distortion
through such points. The book's point at s = 0.03 is below the line through its
neighbours, so it is lifted slightly:

```{r}
#| label: table-blend
LAYER_S <- c(0.0, 0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20)
LAYER_NU <- c(0.02, 0.03, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10)
specified <- (LAYER_S + LAYER_NU) / (1 + LAYER_NU)
blend <- distortion_convex(c(LAYER_S, 1), c(specified, 1))
table_blend <- data.frame(s = as.character(LAYER_S), nu = LAYER_NU, specified = specified,
                          blend = distortion_g(blend, LAYER_S))
gt(table_blend, rowname_col = "s") |>
  tab_header("Table 11.6: the Blend through layer costs of capital", "g(s) at the specified points") |>
  fmt_percent(columns = "nu", decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c("specified", "blend"), decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(nu = "cost of capital", specified = "specified g", blend = "Blend g")
```

```text
      cost of capital  specified g  Blend g
0                  2%       0.0196   0.0000
0.01               3%       0.0388   0.0388
0.03               4%       0.0673   0.0713
0.05               6%       0.1038   0.1038
0.1                8%       0.1667   0.1667
0.2               10%       0.2727   0.2727
```

At s = 0 a distortion is 0 by definition. The specified 0.0196 is the mass at
zero (the rate on line of the most remote layer), which `distortion_mass()`
reports. The Blend is not calibrated, so both books use the same one.

```{r}
")
```

## 7. Pricing each unit with the five distortions

Tables 11.7 and 11.8 price each unit stand-alone under each calibrated
distortion, at its own VaR, and the book total, gross and net. The code compares
premiums only: the pentagon derives the other columns. The last column is the
largest relative gap to the book in the row:

```{r}
#| label: table-117
BOOK_117 <- list( # Table 11.7 (Tame) premiums: A, B, SoP, total; net B, net SoP, net total
  ccoc = c(51.89, 52.98, 104.9, 103.4, 50.98, 102.9, 101.5),
  ph = c(51.90, 52.89, 104.8, 103.4, 50.91, 102.8, 101.8),
  wang = c(51.90, 52.86, 104.8, 103.4, 51.17, 103.1, 102.0),
  dual = c(51.90, 52.83, 104.7, 103.4, 51.44, 103.3, 102.1),
  tvar = c(51.90, 52.81, 104.7, 103.4, 51.63, 103.5, 102.2),
  blend = c(51.05, 51.62, 102.7, 101.9, 50.03, 101.1, 100.5)
)
BOOK_118 <- list( # Table 11.8 (Cat/Non-Cat) premiums: Cat, Non-Cat, SoP, total; net Cat, net SoP, net total
  ccoc = c(34.98, 83.84, 118.8, 115.2, 25.72, 109.6, 105.9),
  ph = c(33.75, 86.36, 120.1, 115.2, 25.11, 111.5, 107.6),
  wang = c(32.82, 87.50, 120.3, 115.2, 25.68, 113.2, 108.8),
  dual = c(31.83, 88.59, 120.4, 115.2, 26.57, 115.2, 110.1),
  tvar = c(31.15, 89.17, 120.3, 115.2, 26.88, 116.0, 110.9),
  blend = c(26.43, 82.39, 108.8, 106.8, 21.17, 103.6, 101.8)
)

by_unit <- function(gross, net, p, distortions, book_values, reinsured, labels, title) {
  rows <- list()
  for (name in names(distortions)) {
    g <- price_stand_alone(gross, distortions[[name]], p)
    n <- price_stand_alone(net, distortions[[name]], p)
    got <- c(g$premium[1:2], g$premium[g$unit == "sum"], g$premium[g$unit == "total"],
             n$premium[reinsured], n$premium[n$unit == "sum"], n$premium[n$unit == "total"])
    book <- book_values[[name]]
    rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- c(got, max(abs(got / book - 1)))
    rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- c(book, NA)
  }
  frame <- data.frame(distortion = interleave(names(distortions)), do.call(rbind, rows), check.names = FALSE)
  names(frame)[-1] <- c(labels, "gap")
  pair_table(frame, setNames(rep(2, length(labels)), labels)) |>
    fmt_percent(columns = "gap", rows = seq(1, nrow(frame), by = 2), decimals = 2) |>
    tab_header(title, "Premiums in currency units") |>
    tab_spanner("gross", columns = labels[1:4]) |>
    tab_spanner("net", columns = labels[5:7])
}

by_unit(tame, tame_net, 0.9999, c(fitted$Tame, list(blend = blend)), BOOK_117, 2,
        c("A", "B", "SoP", "total", "B net", "SoP net", "net total"), "Table 11.7: Tame premiums by distortion")
```

```text
blend        26.43    82.39  108.82  106.76    21.17   103.56     101.82  0.04%
blend, book  26.43    82.39   108.8   106.8    21.17    103.6      101.8
```

Every premium agrees to within one in the book's last printed digit.

By construction, the five distortions charge the gross book the same price. They
disagree about the units alone and about the net book. In Cat/Non-Cat, the Cat
cover (gross minus net premium) is worth 9.3 under the CCoC and 4.3 under TVaR,
so its value depends on the distortion that the capital providers use. The
figure shows both effects (Table 11.8):

```{r}
#| label: cat-cover-figure
cover <- data.frame(
  distortion = factor(rep(names(BOOK_118), 2), levels = names(BOOK_118)),
  panel = rep(c("Cat alone", "Value of the Cat cover"), each = length(BOOK_118)),
  value = c(sapply(BOOK_118, `[`, 1), sapply(BOOK_118, function(b) b[4] - b[7]))
)
cover$panel <- factor(cover$panel, levels = c("Cat alone", "Value of the Cat cover"))
ggplot(cover, aes(distortion, value)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "distortion", y = "currency units (premium; gross less net premium)",
       title = "Cat/Non-Cat: Cat alone and the value of the Cat cover")
```

Exercise 200 asks what reinsurance price is attractive. There is no answer until
you choose the distortion. The Blend is not calibrated, and it charges less than
the others because the cost of its remote capital is low (2% to 10%).

## 8. When an indicator is priced below its expected value

Section 11.7 resolves an apparent paradox. In a portfolio priced by g, the
risk-adjusted probability of "the loss is at most x" is 1 - g(S(x)), below its
true probability F(x). So a policy that pays 1 in good years seems to be priced
below its expected loss.

Stand-alone, this is not true. As its own risk, the indicator is a Bernoulli
with probability F(x), priced at g(F(x)), above F(x). The book uses a lognormal
with mean 10 and CV 0.5 and a PH with rho 0.7:

```{r}
x_loss <- lognormal_from_mean_cv(10, 0.5)
ph7 <- distortion("proportional_hazard", 0.7)
for (p in c(0.5, 0.9)) {
  x0 <- quantile(x_loss, p)
  cat(sprintf("x = %6.3f: P(X <= x) %.2f, stand-alone price %.3f, price as a part of X %.3f\n",
              x0, p, distortion_g(ph7, p), 1 - distortion_g(ph7, 1 - p)))
}
elapsed <- as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), started, units = "secs"))
cat(sprintf("(run time of this guide: %s 15 s)\n", if (elapsed < 15) "under" else "over"))
```

```text
x =  8.944: P(X <= x) 0.50, stand-alone price 0.616, price as a part of X 0.384
x = 16.385: P(X <= x) 0.90, stand-alone price 0.929, price as a part of X 0.800
(run time of this guide: under 15 s)
```

In the portfolio, the indicator pays in the states that the distortion gives
less weight, so it is worth less than its expected value. It is a hedge, and
selling it is like buying reinsurance. Alone, the underwriter orders the states
by the outcome of the indicator and charges a margin. The same difference,
price in a portfolio against price alone, explains the stand-alone columns of
section 7.
